PullRequest.Title: Browser: fix LNA permission query to reflect actual behavior

Scenarios.Scenario: Creating an integrated-browser session and installing Electron permission handlers
Scenarios.CriticalPath: BrowserSession construction synchronously creates BrowserSessionPermissions and installs the existing request/check handlers. The changed permission strings are added to one module-level Set when the module loads; no per-session work or asynchronous prerequisite was added.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Install and later invoke Electron's renderer-to-main permission check/request callbacks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two handlers are installed once per distinct Electron BrowserSession; callback invocations remain driven by page permission checks.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same handlers and Electron callback boundary were installed and invoked before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Handler installation is on session creation, while invocations are on page permission-query/request paths. The diff does not add installations or callback crossings.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of distinct live Electron browser sessions; the changed Set remains a single seven-entry module constant rather than growing per session.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Session construction is synchronous; permission handlers are independently invoked by Electron, with no changed queue, limiter, or concurrency burst.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: BrowserSession instances are reused by Electron session through a WeakMap. The changed module-level Set is initialized once and requires no invalidation, negative caching, or coalescing.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: module ownership and constructor/configure call flow are explicit, and no new startup boundary or per-session allocation is introduced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact session counts vary by scope and workspace, but the diff adds only three constant Set entries once per main-process module load.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: startup work increases by a fixed three-entry Set initialization only, with no realistic user-visible latency or memory scaling.

Scenarios.Scenario: A page calls navigator.permissions.query for local or loopback network access, such as an Okta FastPass preflight
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Blink/Electron synchronously invokes the existing permission check handler. The changed Set membership now returns true immediately; previously the handler continued through URL normalization and category lookup before returning false.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dispatch a web-page permission query from Chromium/Blink to the Electron main-process permission check handler and synchronously return the result.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One existing callback crossing per permission query; adding three recognized values does not multiply queries.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same permission-query callback crossing occurred; local-network strings missed the Set and then performed URL normalization and map lookup before denial.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The callback is the query's critical path, but the changed branch shortens local CPU work and adds no subprocess, filesystem, database, or network operation.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of permission queries issued by loaded pages; each remains one O(1) Set lookup, and the effective permission collection size is fixed at seven.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The check handler is synchronous and each query performs independent constant-time work; no batching or limiter is relevant and the diff creates no aggregate fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No repository-level query cache is involved. Both cold and warm calls use the same immutable Set; no positive/negative cache lifecycle changes.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the exact synchronous handler and before/after branch behavior are directly visible.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Page query frequency is site-dependent, but the changed path is strictly less work than the prior miss path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance finding: the functional grant is a constant-time early return and does not add repeated work or an expensive boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: A page directly requests local-network-access, local-network, or loopback-network permission before accessing an already-allowed local service
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Electron invokes the existing asynchronous request handler, which calls _resolveRequest. The new Set entries resolve true before origin parsing, category mapping, persistence, or prompting, and then invoke the existing callback.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dispatch the renderer permission request to Electron main and invoke the permission callback.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One existing crossing per page permission request; there is no per-origin or per-resource expansion from the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same crossing occurred, followed by local origin/category checks and denial for these unrecognized strings.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The boundary remains on the request critical path, while the new branch avoids store and prompt work rather than adding it.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: The requesting site may proceed with its own local or loopback network access after receiving the intended grant.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Site-defined; the diff does not contain a loop, scheduler, or request fan-out, and Electron already had LocalNetworkAccessChecks disabled.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Electron already allowed local/loopback network access because checks were disabled, although sites that preflighted the permission state could decline to proceed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Any site request is downstream application behavior, not new host-side validation work; the permission result only makes query state match access that was already enabled.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of permission requests a page makes; each remains one Set lookup and one callback, independent of stored origins or browser-session count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Requests may arrive concurrently from pages, but each immediately resolves without prompting; no new Promise fan-out, queue, or unbounded parallel operation is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The immutable allow-list serves warm and cold requests identically. No stored per-origin entries, cache keys, failure retries, or invalidation paths are added.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: _resolveRequest's early return and the absence of storage/prompt/network calls on that branch are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: External sites control downstream network traffic, but there is no changed host mechanism that multiplies or retains that traffic.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression: the diff removes local processing from this request path and merely enables the intended workflow.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over both changed files and all diff pages. Traced module initialization, BrowserSession handler setup, synchronous permission queries, asynchronous permission requests, and downstream boundaries. The three fixed allow-list entries add negligible constant memory and make affected hot paths return earlier; no scalable CPU, memory, I/O, IPC, rendering, cache, cleanup, or concurrency regression was introduced.
